title: Moral Realism and Its Rivals
subtitle: Are there moral facts, or only moral opinions?
objectives: By the end you will be able to distinguish first-order ethics from metaethics and define moral realism precisely.
By the end you will be able to map the main rivals to realism: error theory, relativism, expressivism and constructivism.
By the end you will be able to reconstruct Mackie's argument from relativity and argument from queerness, and assess realist replies.
By the end you will be able to explain the explanatory and evolutionary challenges to realism and the 'companions in guilt' defense.
hook:
Two people argue about whether it is wrong to eat meat. One says it is cruel; the other says animals lack the kind of minds that matter. They might be arguing like two scientists over whether a bridge will hold: one of them is right, and the facts will decide. Or they might be like two diners arguing over whether coriander is delicious: each is reporting a reaction, and there is nothing further to be right about.

Which is it? This is not a question *within* ethics, like the ones you studied when you met Kant's categorical imperative (Day 56) or Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism (Day 61). It is a question *about* ethics: what moral claims mean, whether any are true, and how we could know. That second-order inquiry is called **metaethics**. This track is where the course's moral theories meet their foundations, and this first lesson asks the most basic question of all: are there moral facts?

sections.heading: Mapping the Territory
sections.body:
**First-order** (or normative) ethics asks what is right, good and virtuous. **Metaethics** asks what we are doing when we answer. The distinction matters because people at the same first-order position can differ completely at the metaethical level: two utilitarians can disagree about whether utilitarianism is objectively true.

A useful map uses three questions.

1. **Do moral statements try to describe facts?** If "Torturing for fun is wrong" is the kind of thing that can be true or false, expressing a belief, you are a **cognitivist**. If it instead expresses an attitude, like a cheer or a boo, or a command, you are a **non-cognitivist**. (The next lesson is devoted to non-cognitivism.)
2. **If they try to describe facts, do some succeed?** A cognitivist who says no, every positive moral claim is false, is an **error theorist**.
3. **If some succeed, what makes them true?** If the truth depends on the attitudes or conventions of a culture or person, you hold a form of **relativism** or **subjectivism**. If it is independent of what anyone, or any group, happens to think, you are a **moral realist**.

So **moral realism** is the view that there are moral facts, that some moral claims are true in virtue of them, and that these facts hold independently of what we believe or feel about them. Just as the Earth was round when everyone thought it was flat, slavery was wrong when whole societies approved of it.

Realists themselves divide. **Naturalists** hold that moral facts are natural facts, the kind of thing science could in principle study, such as facts about what promotes human flourishing or satisfies informed desires. The "Cornell realists" (Richard Boyd, Nicholas Sturgeon, David Brink) argued that goodness might be a natural property discovered empirically, much as water turned out to be H₂O. **Non-naturalists**, following G. E. Moore (whom you will meet properly next lesson), hold that moral facts are irreducibly normative: they cannot be identified with any fact of physics, biology or psychology. Recent defenders include Russ Shafer-Landau, David Enoch and Derek Parfit.

Finally, there is a middle path called **constructivism**, associated with Christine Korsgaard and with John Rawls (Day 82). On this view moral truths are not out there waiting to be discovered, but neither are they arbitrary: they are what any rational agent reasoning correctly would be committed to, much as the rules of a game are constructed yet not up to any individual player.

sections.heading: Relativism and the Argument from Disagreement
sections.body:
The oldest rival to realism is **relativism**. The historian Herodotus (5th century BCE) tells a story in his *Histories*. The Persian king Darius asked some Greeks what it would take for them to eat their dead fathers; they replied that nothing would. He then asked the Callatians, an Indian people who did eat their dead, what it would take for them to burn their fathers, as Greeks did; they cried out in horror. Herodotus concluded, quoting the poet Pindar, that custom is king of all. You met a similar idea in Protagoras and the Sophists (Day 8).

The **cultural relativist** holds that "X is wrong" means, or is made true by, the fact that X is forbidden by the speaker's culture. Gilbert Harman's paper "Moral Relativism Defended" (1975) offered a sophisticated version: moral judgments make sense only relative to implicit agreements among a group.

But relativism faces serious objections:
- **The reformer problem.** If right means "approved by my culture," then the abolitionist who said slavery was wrong while her society approved of it was simply mistaken about her own culture. Moral progress becomes impossible to describe; we can only speak of moral change.
- **The disagreement problem.** If I say "Eating meat is wrong" and you say "It isn't," and each of us means "forbidden in my culture" and "not forbidden in mine," then we are not disagreeing at all. Yet it surely feels as though we are.
- **Which culture?** People belong to many groups at once: a nation, a religion, a profession, a family. Relativism does not say which group's code fixes the truth.

Still, the **argument from disagreement** is powerful in another form. J. L. Mackie, in *Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong* (1977), called it the **argument from relativity**. The point is not that disagreement *proves* there is no fact, since people also disagree about science. It is an inference to the best explanation: moral disagreement is so deep and so closely tracks culture and upbringing that the best explanation is that moral views reflect ways of life, not perceptions of an independent moral reality.

Realists reply in two ways. First, much moral disagreement stems from disagreement about non-moral facts (does the fetus feel pain? do sweatshops help the poor?) or from bias and self-interest, which we should expect to distort judgment. Second, beneath the surface variation there is striking agreement: prohibitions on gratuitous cruelty, norms of reciprocity and fairness, care for children. Even Herodotus's story shows two peoples who agree on the deeper principle, honoring the dead, and differ on how to do it.

sections.heading: Mackie's Error Theory and the Argument from Queerness
sections.body:
Mackie opened his book with a blunt sentence: "There are no objective values." But his position is subtle. He agreed with the realist about what ordinary moral language *means*: when we say cruelty is wrong, we mean to state an objective fact, binding on everyone regardless of their desires. He simply thought that this claim to objectivity is false. Moral thought rests on a systematic mistake, so his view is called **error theory**. Compare the atheist's view of statements about the will of Zeus: they are meaningful and aim at truth, but they all fail because there is no Zeus.

Mackie's most famous argument is the **argument from queerness** ("queer" in its older sense of strange). It has two parts.

**Metaphysical queerness.** Objective values would have to be very peculiar entities. A moral fact is supposed to be **intrinsically action-guiding**: knowing that something is wrong is supposed to give anyone a reason not to do it, regardless of what they want. Mackie compared this to Plato's Form of the Good (Day 11), which, once known, would supposedly compel pursuit. Nothing else in the universe, as science describes it, has that kind of built-in "to-be-done-ness." Rocks, electrons and neurons have causal powers, but they do not *demand* anything.

**Epistemological queerness.** If such facts existed, how would we know them? Not by the five senses. We would need a special faculty of **moral intuition**, a kind of perception unlike any other. Mackie found this a lame answer.

A third strand concerns **supervenience**. Moral properties depend on natural ones: if two acts are identical in every natural respect, they cannot differ in rightness. But what explains this necessary link between, say, "causes pain for fun" and "is wrong"? For a non-naturalist, it looks like a brute and mysterious connection between two different kinds of property.

Error theory has an obvious practical question: if all moral claims are false, should we stop making them? Mackie himself went on, in the second half of his book, to propose a practical morality anyway, as a useful human invention. Later, Richard Joyce (*The Myth of Morality*, 2001) developed **moral fictionalism**: we can keep talking as if moral claims were true, as we talk about Sherlock Holmes, because the practice has value.

sections.heading: Explanation and Evolution: Two Modern Challenges
sections.body:
Two newer arguments sharpen Mackie's worries.

**Harman's explanatory challenge.** In *The Nature of Morality* (1977), Harman compared science and ethics. A physicist sees a vapor trail in a cloud chamber and thinks, "There goes a proton." The best explanation of her observation includes the proton. Now you round a corner and see children pouring gasoline on a cat and setting it alight, and you think, "That is wrong." Harman argued that the best explanation of your judgment need not mention any moral fact: your upbringing and psychology explain your reaction perfectly well. If moral facts do no explanatory work, we have no reason to believe in them.

Sturgeon replied (1985) that moral facts do appear in good explanations. Why did Hitler do what he did? Partly because he was morally depraved. Why did opposition to slavery grow in the nineteenth century? Partly, perhaps, because slavery was so obviously unjust that its injustice became harder to ignore. The debate turns on whether such explanations are really moral or merely shorthand for natural facts.

**Street's evolutionary dilemma.** Sharon Street ("A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value," 2006) pointed out that our deepest evaluative tendencies, such as caring for our children, valuing reciprocity, and thinking that pain is bad, were shaped by natural selection, which rewards reproductive success, not tracking independent moral truth. The realist must then choose. Either evolution's influence has no connection to the moral truth, in which case it would be a remarkable coincidence if our values were largely correct, or there is a connection, in which case the realist must explain it, and the simplest explanation (we value what helped our ancestors survive) makes no use of independent moral facts. Realists have replied that the ability to reason, selected for general reasons, could allow us to correct and extend our inherited values, as it allowed us to develop mathematics far beyond anything our ancestors needed.

sections.heading: The Case for Realism
sections.body:
Why, despite all this, did a majority of professional philosophers in the large PhilPapers surveys of 2009 and 2020 accept or lean toward moral realism?

**The appearances.** Moral experience presents itself as objective. When you judge that torturing a child for fun is wrong, you do not experience it as a report of your feelings; you experience it as recognizing something that would be true even if you felt otherwise. Realists, notably Shafer-Landau, hold that we should take appearances at face value unless we have strong reason not to. In the spirit of G. E. Moore's reply to skepticism about the external world (he was more certain that he had hands than of any skeptical premise), some argue that we are more certain that gratuitous cruelty is wrong than we could ever be of the premises of an argument against it.

**Companions in guilt.** This is the realist's strongest counterattack. Mackie's queerness argument targets facts that are intrinsically reason-giving. But **epistemic** norms are like that too. The fact that the evidence strongly supports a hypothesis gives you a reason to believe it, whatever you want. If irreducible reasons are too strange to exist, then there are no facts about what we ought to believe either, and the error theorist's own arguments, which claim we ought to accept their conclusion, undermine themselves. Terence Cuneo (*The Normative Web*, 2007) developed this argument in detail. Mathematics provides another companion: we seem to know necessary, non-physical truths there without any sensory contact with numbers.

**Deliberation.** David Enoch (*Taking Morality Seriously*, 2011) argued that when we deliberate about what to do, we are trying to find the right answer, not simply to discover what we already want. Realism, he argued, is indispensable to the practice of deliberation itself.

Where does that leave us? Each side carries a burden. The realist must explain what moral facts are and how we know them. The anti-realist must explain why morality feels objective, how moral argument and progress are possible, and how to avoid sweeping away epistemic and mathematical facts too. Next lesson, we look at the most ambitious anti-realist strategy: the attempt to explain the meaning of moral language without moral facts at all.

keyQuote.source: J. L. Mackie, Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong (1977), opening sentence of chapter 1

modernConnection.title: Whose Values Should a Machine Learn?
modernConnection.body:
In 2018, a team led by Edmond Awad published results in *Nature* from the **Moral Machine** experiment, an online game that collected around 40 million decisions from people in over 200 countries and territories about how a self-driving car should act in unavoidable crashes. Should it spare the young over the old, many over few, pedestrians over passengers? Some preferences were broadly shared, such as sparing humans over animals and more lives over fewer. But there were also marked regional differences, for instance in how strongly people favored sparing the young.

This is the argument from disagreement in data form, and it bears directly on a practical problem: **AI alignment**, the project of making artificial systems act in accordance with human values. If a company trains an AI model to be "good," what is the target? A relativist might say: the values of the culture where it is deployed, which raises the reformer problem in a new form (should an AI deployed in a society that tolerates discrimination tolerate it too?). An error theorist might say there is no moral target to hit, only preferences to aggregate, and the real question is whose preferences get counted. A realist might say there is a fact about what is right, which we should try to approximate through reasoning, with data on human opinion serving only as evidence, sometimes poor evidence.

AI developers have in fact adopted different strategies: learning from human ratings, writing explicit principles, or consulting the public on what rules should govern a system. Each strategy embeds a metaethical bet, even when no one names it. The Moral Machine authors were careful to say that their data should inform, not settle, policy, which is itself a recognition that what people prefer and what is right may come apart. Whether they can come apart is precisely the question this lesson has explored.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of philosophy that asks what moral claims mean, whether they can be true, and how we could know them.
vocabulary.example: Asking whether 'stealing is wrong' states a fact is a metaethical question; asking whether stealing is wrong is not.

vocabulary.definition: The view that there are moral facts that hold independently of what anyone believes or feels, and that some moral claims are true in virtue of them.
vocabulary.example: A moral realist holds that slavery was wrong even when whole societies approved of it.

vocabulary.definition: The view that moral statements express beliefs and are capable of being true or false.
vocabulary.example: Both the realist and the error theorist are cognitivists: they agree moral claims aim at truth.

vocabulary.definition: J. L. Mackie's view that moral claims aim to state objective facts but are all false because there are no such facts.
vocabulary.example: An error theorist treats 'murder is wrong' like a claim about witches: meaningful but untrue.

vocabulary.definition: Mackie's argument that objective values would be metaphysically and epistemologically strange, unlike anything else in the universe.
vocabulary.example: The argument from queerness asks how a fact could, all by itself, give everyone a reason to act.

vocabulary.definition: The view that moral claims are true or false only relative to the norms of a particular culture.
vocabulary.example: A cultural relativist would say that burning the dead is right for the Greeks and wrong for the Callatians.

vocabulary.definition: A relation of dependence: moral properties cannot differ between two cases unless some natural property differs too.
vocabulary.example: If two acts are alike in every natural detail, supervenience says they must be alike in rightness.

vocabulary.definition: A defense of realism arguing that anti-realist objections would equally eliminate other respectable normative facts, such as epistemic reasons.
vocabulary.example: The companions in guilt argument notes that 'you ought to believe the evidence' is just as normative as 'you ought not to lie'.

thinkingExercise.title: Locate Yourself on the Map
thinkingExercise.prompt: Use a single moral conviction you hold strongly to discover your own metaethical position.
steps: Write down one moral claim you are very confident of (for example, 'It is wrong to humiliate someone for entertainment').
Imagine a society that sincerely approved of the practice. Would your claim still be true there? Write down your answer and why.
Ask whether your claim would be true if every human being, including you, came to approve of the practice. If yes, you lean realist; if no, you lean toward relativism or subjectivism.
Pick the anti-realist argument from this lesson you find hardest to answer (disagreement, queerness, explanation or evolution) and write the best reply you can.
Check for consistency: do you also believe there are facts about what we ought to believe given the evidence? If so, does the companions in guilt argument move you?

summary: Metaethics asks what moral claims mean and whether they can be true; moral realism holds that there are mind-independent moral facts.

Rivals include relativism (truth relative to a culture), error theory (all moral claims false), non-cognitivism (moral claims express attitudes) and constructivism (morality is what correct practical reasoning yields).

Mackie's argument from relativity treats deep disagreement as best explained by differing ways of life; his argument from queerness says objective, intrinsically action-guiding values would be metaphysically and epistemically strange.
Harman's explanatory challenge and Street's evolutionary dilemma question whether moral facts are needed to explain our moral beliefs.
Realists appeal to the appearance of objectivity, to companions in guilt such as epistemic reasons, and to the presuppositions of deliberation.

quiz.question: Which of these is a metaethical question rather than a first-order ethical one?
options: Is it wrong to eat meat?
Should we give more to charity?
Do moral statements state facts that can be true or false?
Is lying permissible to save a life?
quiz.explanation: Metaethics asks about the nature and status of moral claims. The others ask what is actually right or wrong.

quiz.question: J. L. Mackie's error theory holds that:
options: Moral claims aim to state objective facts but are all false
Moral claims express emotions rather than beliefs
Moral claims are true relative to a culture
Moral claims are true when they maximize happiness
quiz.explanation: Mackie agreed that moral language aims at objective truth, but he argued that there are no objective values for it to describe.

quiz.question: According to the argument from queerness, objective moral facts would be strange partly because they would have to give everyone a reason to act regardless of their desires.
quiz.explanation: Mackie's metaphysical point is that such intrinsic action-guidingness has no parallel in the natural world.

quiz.question: An abolitionist in 1830 says slavery is wrong although her society approves of it. Which view has the most trouble saying she was right?
options: Non-naturalist realism
Naturalist realism
Constructivism
Cultural relativism
quiz.explanation: If 'wrong' means 'disapproved of by my culture', she was simply mistaken. This is the reformer problem.

quiz.question: Harman's explanatory challenge claims that:
options: Moral facts explain why evolution occurred
Our moral observations can be fully explained without mentioning moral facts
Moral facts are identical to natural facts
Moral disagreement is always about non-moral facts
quiz.explanation: Unlike the proton in the cloud chamber, the wrongness of burning the cat seems unnecessary to explain why we judge it wrong.

quiz.question: Sharon Street's Darwinian dilemma argues that natural selection has made our moral beliefs reliably track mind-independent moral truth.
quiz.explanation: Street argues the opposite: selection aims at reproductive success, so it would be a coincidence if our evolved values matched independent moral facts.

quiz.question: The 'companions in guilt' reply to Mackie points out that:
options: Mackie himself was a moral realist
Epistemic reasons to believe the evidence are as normatively 'queer' as moral reasons
Most cultures agree about morality
Evolution supports realism
quiz.explanation: If irreducibly normative facts cannot exist, there would be no facts about what we ought to believe either, which undercuts the anti-realist's own arguments.

quiz.question: Cornell realists such as Richard Boyd held that moral properties might be natural properties discovered empirically, as water was discovered to be H₂O.
quiz.explanation: This is naturalist realism: moral facts are part of the natural world, though not identical by definition to any simple descriptive term.

quiz.question: A company decides its AI should follow whatever moral views are most popular in each country where it operates. Which metaethical position does this policy most closely reflect?
options: Cultural relativism
Non-naturalist realism
Error theory
Constructivism
quiz.explanation: Tying rightness to local majority norms is the practical form of cultural relativism, and it inherits the reformer problem.

goDeeper.body:
A powerful contemporary development is the debate over **robust** versus **quietist** realism. Robust realists like Enoch and Parfit (in *On What Matters*, 2011) accept that moral facts are irreducibly normative and that this is a substantive metaphysical commitment, to be defended against Mackie with arguments from deliberation and companions in guilt. **Quietist** realists, such as Ronald Dworkin in his paper "Objectivity and Truth: You'd Better Believe It" (1996) and later in *Justice for Hedgehogs* (2011), argue instead that the metaphysical questions themselves are confused. To say "slavery is wrong, and objectively so, and would be wrong even if everyone approved" is simply to make further moral claims. There is no neutral, external standpoint, outside morality, from which to ask whether moral facts "really exist." On this view the skeptic is not doing metaphysics but bad ethics.

Parfit made a related move: he held that normative truths, like mathematical truths, are true without having any **ontological** implications. They do not exist in some spooky realm; they are simply true, as "there is a prime number between 5 and 9" is true without numbers being located anywhere.

Critics, including many expressivists you will meet next lesson, reply that this sounds suspiciously like their own position. If realism makes no metaphysical claims, how does it differ from a sophisticated anti-realism that also lets us say "slavery is objectively wrong" in an ordinary voice? This convergence, or apparent convergence, between quietist realism and quasi-realism is one of the liveliest puzzles in current metaethics.

readings.author: J. L. Mackie
readings.note: Chapter 1 contains the arguments from relativity and queerness and remains admirably clear.

readings.title: Moral Realism: A Defence
readings.author: Russ Shafer-Landau
readings.note: A careful non-naturalist defense that replies to each major anti-realist argument.

readings.title: A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value
readings.author: Sharon Street
readings.note: The influential 2006 article in Philosophical Studies that launched the evolutionary debunking debate.

readings.title: Metaethics: A Contemporary Introduction
readings.author: Mark van Roojen
readings.note: A balanced textbook covering every position on this lesson's map.

questions: Does the existence of moral progress (for example, the abolition of slavery) give us evidence for moral realism?
If evolution explains why we think pain is bad, does that make the belief less likely to be true, or not?
Could you live as a consistent error theorist? What would change in how you speak and act?
